Last lesson this room put back $425,000 a week into its own clubs, with no rule at all. Under the old rule this room did not replace, it put back $0 a week. Effort went down by $425,000 a week. Both figures are DOLLARS, because the two lessons' dials are percentages of different money. 6 desks put back fewer dollars a week than they did last lesson and 0 put back more — and nothing about the rule made trying less worth it. The arrows at stage 4 say this rule moved nobody's best move. Ask the question, take the answers, and do not name moral hazard at all in this room — the instrument does not support it.

[teach:consequence:ask]
Whose effort went down? Under this rule nobody's best move changed at any desk — so what made it fall?

[stage 4 arrow line]
The rule this room ended up with did not move a single dial. The best price and the best thing to put back are exactly where they were with no rule at all, at all 6 desks. At 60% — the number this room argued about and did not pass — 4 of 6 desks would have moved, the biggest by 4 clicks of the dial. That is what the room decided not to do.

[teacher ASK answer]
Do NOT fish for moral hazard here. This room's own arrows say the rule changed nobody's best price and nobody's best reinvest, so putting money back never stopped being worth it — these desks put back less anyway. Say that out loud: the fall is theirs, not the rule's. Then ask what the rule would have had to be to change anybody's best move — stage 4's counterfactual column has that number.
